raw_evidence.label: What the dataset is and where it comes from
raw_evidence.content: This dataset compares the University of Oxford and the University of Cambridge as producers of two kinds of elite Britons: Prime Ministers and Nobel laureates. It was built on 2026-05-24 by querying the free Wikidata SPARQL endpoint. Prime Ministers are everyone who has held the position 'Prime Minister of the United Kingdom' (Wikidata Q14211), filtered to real humans (instance of Q5) to strip out fictional PMs that Wikidata also lists, such as Harriet Jones from Doctor Who and Francis Urquhart from House of Cards. University attribution uses the 'educated at' (P69) property and follows the 'part of' (P361) chain, so attending a constituent college such as Christ Church or Trinity counts toward the parent university. The dataset is a clean, reproducible snapshot rather than an official record, and the headline split it captures is one of the most durable facts in British public life.

The concentration is extreme even within Cambridge: Trinity College alone claims around 34 Nobel laureates, more than the entire University of Oxford on some counts. The Cavendish Laboratory, home to the discovery of the electron, the neutron and the structure of DNA, anchors this tradition. The mirror-image specialisation — Oxford for statesmen, Cambridge for scientists — is exactly the division the dataset measures, though the dataset's own counts (30 Oxford vs 79 Cambridge) are lower because they use only Wikidata 'educated at' links rather than the broader 'affiliated with' definitions used by university PR.

raw_evidence.label: Why Oxford produces so many Prime Ministers
raw_evidence.content: Oxford's grip on Downing Street is not random — it is institutional. The Sutton Trust attributes it to three reinforcing mechanisms. First, the Oxford Union, founded in 1823 and described as a 'children's House of Commons', is where future politicians learn to debate and build networks; at least 12 Prime Ministers learned their trade there, including Gladstone, Macmillan, Heath, Johnson and May. Second, the Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE) degree, created in the 1920s, became the de facto training course for British political life — three of the last six Prime Ministers studied PPE, and 24 MPs in the last parliament held the degree. Third, an institutional division of identity: since the early 20th century Oxford positioned itself as the university of humanities and politics while Cambridge leaned toward science and technology, steering politically ambitious students one way and scientifically ambitious students the other. This is the causal story behind the numbers in the data.

raw_evidence.content: Oxford's grip on Downing Street is not random — it is institutional. The Sutton Trust attributes it to three reinforcing mechanisms. First, the Oxford Union, founded in 1823 and described as a 'children's House of Commons', is where future politicians learn to debate and build networks; at least 12 Prime Ministers learned their trade there, including Gladstone, Macmillan, Heath, Johnson and May. Second, the Philosophy, Politics and Economics (PPE) degree, created in the 1920s, became the de facto training course for British political life — three of the last six Prime Ministers studied PPE, and 24 MPs in the last parliament held the degree. Third, an institutional division of identity: since the early 20th century Oxford positioned itself as the university of humanities and politics while Cambridge leaned toward science and technology, steering politically ambitious students one way and scientifically ambitious students the other. This is the causal story behind the numbers in the data.
